I should like to write out the types of man, one by one. It was from a motive of that sort, I feel, that I became a writer of novels. Never once have I carried any grand notion of "literature," or of "art," about the work (whether a novel is, properly speaking, an art at all).

To grasp in my own way this creature called man, so tragic and yet so utterly comic, I must have a historical age to do it in. For their lives are complete, finished. Between them and the writer there lies that convenient distance called time, across which one may test and probe and hold a man up to the light at leisure.

It is just on a hundred years now since the life of the man Hijikata Toshizō was completed. This man lived through the last convulsive years of the shogunate. He made the Shinsengumi, a strange body with no likeness before it or after it in the history of Japan, and set it to work, worked it too hard indeed, and while leaving on history a scar without parallel he spent his whole life to that one end and no other. For what place in history, one wonders, was he born to fill?

I do not know. Toshizō himself can hardly have known. He only strained his spirit to the utmost and lived in a kind of rapture. That absurdity is, I suppose, the thing fated to men of his kind. The more feverishly his spirit ran hot, the more comic he grew, and in the same motion he found himself playing out a tragedy heavy with feeling.
Ishida, in the post-town of Hino in Bushū: that is the village where this man was born.

The place-name now reads Ishida, Hino City, in the Tokyo Metropolitan district; but apart from a little modern building that has gone up here and there nearby, the scene is much as it was when he was born. It is farmland of the black, crumbly loam peculiar to the Musashino plain, thick with copses of miscellaneous trees.
I visited the house of his birth twice. In a village of pleasing aspect there stands a large farmhouse.
"The rich folk's house? That would be over yonder,"

so a young man of the village pointed me to the Hijikata house, in just that manner of speaking. The present head of the family, a mild man past his middle years, a great-grandson of Toshizō's elder brother, received me.
"Yes, hereabouts he was always called Toshi-san, Toshi-san."
There is a great central pillar in the house. At about four shaku up, the wood glowed a deep amber. The pillar stands close by the bath-room.
"When he came up out of the bath, they say, Toshi-san would set himself against this pillar and practice his sumō."
In the garden grows arrow-bamboo.

"He planted that, so we are told. A strange child he must have been. A peasant's son, and yet he would say that he was going to become a samurai. Yes, arrow-bamboo was always planted at a samurai's residence, they say, so no doubt he was copying it."

In this, his birth-house, Toshizō had left behind a sword by Izumi-no-kami Kanesada, said to be the one he carried in the Kyoto years, along with the brow-plate of a helmet and a few other things. On the brow-plate there was a sword-cut.
The Satō house, whose head is a great-grandson of Toshizō's elder sister, stands along the Kōshū highway in Hino. Its master,
"After the Restoration we had a hard time holding our heads up, my grandmother used to say,"
he told me with a smile; and of all the family it was his features that came nearest to Toshizō's face in the photograph.
"A cool, clear look about the eyes, they say, a face like an actor's."
For some days I walked here and there about his native country.

On the dry bed of the Asakawa, a tributary of the Tama River, I even tried my hand at picking the thorny medicinal herb. As a boy, they say, he would direct the villagers in the family trade of gathering it; and it struck me that his genius for organization might well have been born of just such experience of labor.
"Very likely so, yes,"

the head of the Hijikata house agreed. He explained to me in detail, too, the whole process, from the gathering of the herb to the making of the medicine. To direct a hundred people or so, divided station by station and moving about in a complicated dance, takes very considerable skill, he said.

Toshizō was a man who possessed a new sense, the sense of organization, that no Japanese before him had had; and the concrete work he made of it was, it seems to me, the Shinsengumi. In that sense alone, may we not say that this man's passion and talent brought off a work belonging to the history of culture itself?
Shiba Ryōtarō
